answer: Use the sc-rx (Receiving Secure Channel) show command: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the one that tells you whether the channel is carrying traffic; it is returned by the MKA stack and has two values: in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and not-in-use, meaning no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use. The key is name (string, length 0..64) plus index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel object and it is read-only: the only form is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. There is no add, set or delete for sc-tx, so you cannot configure it. It is keyed by name (string, length 0..64) and index, the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is reported by the MKA stack as in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign the certificate with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>, for example set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client; multiple certificates are given as a comma list, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. id is a string of length 0..20 and active-certificate-id a string of length 0..128. show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert] reports which one is actually in-use (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id), the type (server or client) and status (enabled or disabled); show secure-applications lists them all. To demand a client certificate, set verify-client-cert, which enables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled (default) means no client certificate is requested, required means the client certificate is required and validated. Changes take effect only for new TLS connections.

That depends on re-key-fail-policy on the secure entity. It indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful, and takes kill-traffic or continue-traffic, defaulting to continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. Both are settable with add secure-entity-<name> ... or set secure-entity-<name> [re-key-frequency <value>] [re-key-fail-policy <value>] [traffic-kill-offset <value>]. Related, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer, 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. Example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is a show-only object with a single fixed proposal: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. There is no add or set form. Every attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: number is 1, encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521. The integrity-algorithm and dh-group are the values advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. What you can tune on the encryption entity itself is the secure-entity re-key behaviour, not the algorithm suite.

Through the security-policy-database (SPD), which is keyed by the local IKE instance and the peer and carries the secure entity as an attribute: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (the IKE SA); both are strings. associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). You can also use set to change it, show security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity] to read it, and delete security-policy-database-<...> to remove the entry. Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with a manually configured CRL Distribution Point. Each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Configure it with add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], and adjust later with set cdp-<name> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) enables automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or update is performed but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval is either the special enum use-next-update, which takes the next refresh time from the current CRL next-update field, or a duration written as [xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs], for example 2w, 5d 12h, or 1h 7m 30s. show cdp-<name> also reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result; show cdps lists all. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. days is the number of days the certificate is valid for and defaults to 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string 1..64, common-name the IP or host name that identifies the server (1..64), and subject the full certificate subject name (1..1024); when generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true, false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. -f forces the command without confirmation. The command runs in Operational mode. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly. Create one with add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. map-type is extract or map. field applies only when map-type is extract and names the certificate attribute used to determine identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn, san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked, priority ranges 1 to 255, and issuer (value any) restricts the rule to certificates from a specific issuer in the trust chain. enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Delete it with clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, which removes already imported local, trusted or peer X509v3 certificates. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID (string, length 0..128) which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to get the list of certificate-ids that can be cleared. type also accepts the bulk options purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. Without -f you are prompted Are you sure? [y/n]. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY, clear certificate trusted id=root. To see what is installed, run show certificates, which displays all managed local, trusted and peer X509v3 certificates imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations. Access is Operational mode.

Use the clear crl command with a clear-target rather than naming each CRL: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. The targets are single-crl (the default, which removes only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension), and purge-all-crls (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale ones, use clear crl purge-invalid-crls; use <tab> to list clearable CRL names. -f forces without confirmation. Check first with show crls or show crl-<name>, where status is valid, expired or future and type is cached or manually. Example: clear crl single-crl myCA-1. Clear runs in Operational mode; show is also available in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the pending-import state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then signed by an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded back into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that download happens, show local-certificate-<id> reports status pending-import, meaning the certificate was generated by CSR but import is not yet complete. Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256; signature-hash-algorithm defaults to sha256 for rsa2048, rsa3072 and eccp256, sha384 for eccp384, sha512 for rsa4096 and eccp521. metadata-template defaults to generic. The subject CN RDN is mandatory. Runs in Operational mode. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type defines the requested type of display operation and accepts all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details and certificate-hierarchy, with all-certificate-hierarchy as the default. So chain views are what you get by default; pass display-type=certificate-details when you want only that certificate's own fields. The certificate parameter is the certificate to display, given by its full name such as trusted-certificate-ca_root, local-certificate-server_cert or local-certificate-pace_client; pressing <tab> at certificate= lists the available names. The command also displays CSR details. Output includes version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity Not Before / Not After, subject, public key info and X509v3 extensions. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS and replaces the complex manual CSR process; the device includes an EST client that talks to a dedicated EST server. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [metadata-from-certificate=]<value> [metadata-from-cnf=]<value> [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca defaults to 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>], read back with show est-ca-<name>. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA. It takes a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the not-after minus not-before interval rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%, or disabled. The default is Disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until you configure it. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example through expiration. The CA is pinned by explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, which verifies the Root CA identity using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to secure the initial connection. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is set by server-port and defaults to 443. Configure servers with add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], and change them with set est-server-<name>/<server-name> [...] or remove them with delete est-server-<name>/<server-name>. Yes, you can define more than one: priority defines the server's precedence with a value range of 1 to 10, and if omitted the priority defaults to the current lowest precedence (the highest existing number) plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. server-address is the IP address of the EST server. enabled is True or False, defaulting to True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. passphrase decodes encrypted input certificates and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for a single certificate it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example issuer /CN=Nokia yields trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. import-certificate -h displays help. Runs in Operational mode. Example: import-certificate peer-certificate certificate-name=peer-cert1 <string in PEM format>.

Check the ISK attributes before clearing. show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates if the key is in use in this FRU (true, false, default false), is-key-verified indicates if the key is verified in this FRU (true, false, default false), and being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, indicating deletion is in progress and the ISK will soon be removed. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one, use clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where the name of the key to be deleted must be provided; key-name is a string of length 0..64 and -f forces without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name.

Use show KRKs to list all Image Root Keys on the system, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] for a single one. KRK is read-only; there is no add, set or clear form. name is the unique representation of the object, CPU is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0 (uint8), key-name is the key name (string, length 0..64), key-serial-number is the Key Serial Number, issuer-name is the name of the CSA, or Code Signing Appliance (string, length 0..20), key-length is the key length in bits (uint16), and key-payload is the key payload in hex format (string, length 0..1100). Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1.

Use show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. It is show-only. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and takes not-installed, installing, installed or failed. KRP-version is the package version, issuer-name is the name of the CSA, or Code Signing Appliance (string, length 0..20), and KRK-name is the name of the KRK, the Image Root Key, that signed this ISK. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512, signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none, signature-payload is a hex string of 0..1024, and signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on the local certificate: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. Setting force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked regardless of CRL or OCSP results; force-unrevoked does the opposite. The id is a string of length 1..128 matching the pattern ([A-Za-z0-9_.,/@][A-Za-z0-9_-.,/@]*). Read it back with show local-certificate-<id> [...] [status] [revocation-mode] [used-by] [...]; status reports revoked among values such as valid, expired, untrusted, future and pending-import, and used-by lists the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and other objects presently using the certificate. The same revocation-mode attribute with the same values and default exists on peer-certificate. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Add it with add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], then adjust with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] or remove it with delete ocsp-server-<name>. priority sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, and the range is uint8 1..10, so priority 1 is tried first. name is a string of length 0..64. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form http://<host>[:<port>], where host may be an IPv4 or IPv6 address or a DNS name, and if the port is omitted the default HTTP port 80 is used; the string is 0..1024 with pattern http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*). enabled controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status, true or false, default false. show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query] also reports last-query, the timestamp of the last successful query. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application. Its white-listed attribute is read-only and takes true or false, defaulting to false. If true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain, listed in trust-chain as a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. View it with show peer-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] [...] [white-listed] [alarm-report-control] [label] [...]. What you can change is set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]: revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked with default auto, and alarm-report-control is inhibited or allowed with default allowed. status values include valid, revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future and unsupported.

SSH direct shell access listens on port 8022 by default and is off by default. Both are attributes of the ssh object: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>], read back with show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. enabled enables direct access to shell via ssh and takes true or false, defaulting to false. port is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell, a number in the range 1..65535, default 8022. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440, with no default. post-login-message is displayed after user login, also 0..1440, and defaults to a Warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Use add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]; change the label with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], view it with show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and remove it with delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>, which prompts for confirmation. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user (string 0..32); key-id is a unique identifier for the entry (string 1..64). public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format as <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded OpenSSH public key<SPACE><comment>, up to 2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is read-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTIt...
